title: Tirumangai Āzhwār
body:
The Chōḻa kingdom, famed for its beauty and wealth, was made up of many smaller territories. Among them was Tiruvāli Nāḍu, also known as Tiruvāli Tirunagari, a land of lakes and flower-filled groves that captured the heart of every visitor.

In this land lay a small village called Tirukkuraiyalūr, where devotees of Sriman Nārāyaṇa lived and spoke always of His glory. There lived Ālināḍār, the commander of the Chōḻa army, and his wife Vallittiru. They lived peacefully and were deeply devoted to Sriman Nārāyaṇa.

In reward for their bhakti and their virtuous life, in the year Naḷa, in the month of Kārthigai, on Pournami, a Thursday, under the Kārthigai nakshatram, around the eighth century, a son was born to them as an amśam of the Śārngam, the bow of Sriman Nārāyaṇa and one of His five divine weapons. They named him Nīlan.

From childhood Nīlan received a sound education, including the study of Sanskrit. Born into a line of warriors, he mastered the sword and the bow, and learned to command all four divisions of an army: the elephants, the cavalry, the chariots and the foot soldiers. Hearing of his intelligence and his valour, the Chōḻa king made him commander of his forces.

At that time there lived a celebrated poet who bore the title Nāṛkavip Perumāl, having defeated every rival in poetic contests. Hearing of Nīlan, he challenged him to a contest. But Nīlan was every bit as accomplished a poet, and after an exchange of many verses, the poet conceded defeat. From then on, the Chōḻa king conferred the title Nāṛkavip Perumāl upon Nīlan himself.

Nīlan led the Chōḻa forces into battle and defeated their enemies. In recognition of his bravery, the Chōḻa king made him ruler of Āli Nāḍu, with its capital at Tirumangai. His prowess in war made enemy kings regard him as Kālan, Death himself, and so he was also given the name Parakālan, "the one beyond the reach of Death." Though his name was Nīlan, once he became king of Tirumangai he was known throughout the Chōḻa land as Tirumangai Mannan.

The Curse of Sumangali

At that time, in Dēvalōkam, there lived a celestial maiden named Sumangali, foremost among the Dēva kanyās. Once she wished to visit the earth, and with the other celestial maidens she came down first to the Himālayas. There Kapila Muni was expounding the glory of Sriman Nārāyaṇa to a large gathering of sages and devotees. Among the sages was one whose face and body were disfigured. Seeing him, the celestial maidens, and Sumangali in particular, mocked him and laughed. Angered by their conduct, Kapila Muni cursed Sumangali to be born as a mortal woman on earth and to become the wife of a mortal man.

Sumangali was stricken and realised her mistake. She begged Kapila Muni to withdraw the curse.

Seeing her remorse, Kapila Muni explained that a curse once given could not be taken back, for it was destined, but he offered her a way. She would marry a great warrior of keen intellect, an amśam of the Śārngam, the bow of Sriman Nārāyaṇa, who would be king of Tirumangai in the Chōḻa land. His mind, he said, was wholly given to war; she must turn it towards herself, and from there towards devotion to Sriman Nārāyaṇa. When she had done so, she would return to the celestial world. Hearing this, Sumangali was content.

Sumangali and the other maidens then went to Tirunāngūr, where they were drawn to a pond covered with alli flowers. Enchanted, they went down into the water and bathed. When the time came to leave, the other maidens departed without her. Sumangali searched for her companions in vain and understood that all of this was unfolding as destined. She took the form of a newborn infant and lay among the flowers of the pond.

Nearby lived a skilled physician who had no children of his own. Passing by the pond, he found the infant and rejoiced, believing her to be a gift from the Lord. He took her home, where his wife too was overjoyed. They named her Kumudavalli and raised her with great love.

Kumudavalli's Conditions

Years passed, and one day her father told Kumudavalli that she had come of age to marry, and asked what she wished. She then revealed the secret of her birth and told him that she was destined to marry Tirumangai Mannan, who would himself come to seek her hand.

In time, Tirumangai Mannan heard of Kumudavalli's beauty and resolved to meet her and marry her. He rode to Tirunāngūr with his soldiers on his horse, Āḍalmā, and sent word to the physician that Tirumangai Mannan had come to seek his daughter's hand.

Kumudavalli came before Tirumangai Mannan, and the two were drawn to each other. But she set a condition: she would marry him only if he dedicated his life to Emperumān and to the service of the devotees of Sriman Nārāyaṇa. He accepted. Setting aside the bearing of a king, he became a humble devotee of Sriman Nārāyaṇa, adorned himself with the Tirumaṇ before Tirunaraiyūr Nambi at Tirunaraiyūr, and returned to the physician's house.

Kumudavalli then made one more request. She had vowed to feed a hundred Bhāgavatas, devotees of Sriman Nārāyaṇa, to wash their feet, and to sprinkle that water upon her own head. If he would fulfil this too, she would gladly marry him. He agreed to this as well, consulted the priests, and fixed an auspicious day, and on that day they were married.

From then on, Tirumangai Mannan pledged to feed one thousand and eight Bhāgavatas every day. As the days went by, the cost of this service drained his treasury, and he could no longer pay the kappam, the tribute owed by a subordinate king to the emperor.

The Chōḻa king, angered, sent soldiers to collect it, but Parakālan, having spent his wealth on the devotees of Sriman Nārāyaṇa, could not pay. At last the king sent a great army against him, but Parakālan, brave and well supported, could not be defeated. The king then reproached him: after all the honours bestowed upon him, this was how he repaid them. It grieved the king, and he would not let it happen again. If Parakālan failed to pay, he warned, he would face the consequences.

The Wedding Party in the Forest

Parakālan then resolved to take wealth from others by force and use it to serve the devotees of Sriman Nārāyaṇa. Seeing his mind turn this way, Emperumān resolved to transform him. Sriman Nārāyaṇa and Periya Pirāṭṭi, Sri Mahālakshmi, took the form of a newly wedded couple and passed through the forest where Tirumangai Mannan waylaid wealthy travellers and seized their jewels and money. He and his men stopped the wedding party and ordered everyone to hand over their jewels and wealth.

Everyone obeyed, the bridegroom and the bride among them. Tirumangai Mannan checked that every ornament had been surrendered, and noticed that the bridegroom still wore a ring upon his foot. He demanded that it too be removed. The bridegroom replied that he could not remove it, and that Parakālan was welcome to try. Nīlan tried and failed; he even tried to pull it off with his teeth, and still he could not. Marvelling that this stranger was as strong as himself, he called him Kaliyan, the mighty one. In truth, it was so that Kaliyan might come into contact with the sacred feet of Sriman Nārāyaṇa, and that this might be revealed to the world, that all of this took place.

Leaving the ring, he ordered his chief soldier, Thōḷā Vazhakkan, to tie up the jewels and wealth and carry them away. But the soldier could not lift the bundle. Tirumangai Mannan tried, and he too failed.

Angered, he accused the bridegroom of casting a spell to make the bundle immovable. The Lord, in the guise of the bridegroom, asked Kaliyan to come close so that He might explain the mantram. Then Perumāl whispered into his right ear the Ashṭākshara mantram, which shone before his eyes like light. From that moment Tirumangai Mannan became Tirumangai Āzhwār. He recognised the bridegroom and bride as none other than Emperumān and Sri Mahālakshmi, and he was lost in the meaning of the mantram.

His eyes flooded with tears, his hands rose above his head in worship, and he began to sing the praise of Perumāl:

"Kulam tharum, selvam thandhiḍum,
aḍiyār paḍuthuyar āyinavellām
nilantharam seyyum, nīḷ visumbaruḷum,
aruḷoḍu perunilam aḷikkum,
valam tharum, maṭrum thandhiḍum, peṭra
thāyinum āyina seyyum;
nalam tharum sollai nān
kaṇḍukoṇḍēn, Nārāyaṇā ennum nāmam."

"It grants status and bestows wealth; it levels to the ground every sorrow that besets His devotees; it grants the vast heavens and, with grace, the wide earth; it gives strength and all good things besides; it does more than even a mother who bore us would do. I have found that word which bestows all good: the name Nārāyaṇa."

Here "the earth" means not only land as property, but the ground on which a person comes to be recognised.

The Āzhwār sang ten Pāsurams in praise of Sriman Nārāyaṇa. Hearing them, Perumāl gave His darśanam with Sri Mahālakshmi upon Garuḍa, and asked the Āzhwār to sing His glory at His many kshethrams. Then He vanished from sight.
